body.text: Few places or corridors tell a richer story of geography and human movement than Uluburun shipwreck. Stepping into its history reveals how trade, terrain, and culture shaped the modern map.

Uluburun ("Grand Cape" in Turkish) is a Late Bronze Age underwater archaeological site, located in the Mediterranean Sea south of Kaş, in Turkey where a shipwreck dated to the late 14th century BC was discovered.
The sunken ship, approximately 15 meters long and carrying a cargo of over 20 tons, was lying at a depth of over 40 meters at the time of its discovery.

The shipwreck was discovered in the summer of 1982 by Mehmed Çakir, a local sponge diver from Yalıkavak, a village near Bodrum, and was subsequently excavated, from 1984 to 1994. It yielded a large quantity of very diverse objects.

Its main cargoes were ingots of copper and tin (for bronze making), jars of terebinth resin, painted ceramics, and raw glass. But it also yielded various luxury items, personal effects, and utilitarian objects.

At the time of its sinking, the ship was sailing from the east, probably the Levant (Near East) and/or Cyprus, westward toward the Aegean Sea, likely toward a city of the Mycenaean civilization in present-day Greece.
In addition to its crew, merchants of Levantine (Canaanite) origin were on the ship, as well as people from Greece, or even further north in the Balkans.

Since its discovery, the Uluburun shipwreck has been the subject of numerous studies, whether analyses of its cargo or proposals on its economic or even political significance. It is certainly not the oldest shipwreck discovered in the Mediterranean, but it is the one with the richest cargo.

It sheds light on the long-distance exchange of goods during a period of the Late Bronze Age, for which they were already extensively studied from the archives of el-Amarna in Egypt and Ugarit in Syria.

The cargo carried by the ship is generally considered to have been intended for a wealthy and powerful individual or group, perhaps a Mycenaean king, or at least a royal institution and members of the elite.

It is however impossible to determine whether these were gifts sent as part of diplomatic relations, or goods bought through private commercial transactions by merchants on behalf of a sponsor (or both).
Discovery and excavation

The shipwreck site was discovered in the summer of 1982 due to Mehmet Çakir's sketching of "the metal biscuits with ears" recognized as oxhide ingots. Turkish sponge divers were often consulted by the Institute of Nautical Archaeology's (INA) survey team on how to identify ancient wrecks while diving for sponges.

Çakir's findings urged Oğuz Alpözen, Director of the Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology, to send out an inspection team of the Museum and INA archaeologists to locate the wreck site. The inspection team was able to locate several amounts of copper ingots just 50 metres from the shore of Uluburun.

The Institute of Nautical Archaeology (INA) began excavating in July 1984 under the direction of its founder, George F. Bass, and was then turned over to INA's vice president for Turkey, Cemal Pulak, who directed the excavation from 1985 to 1994.
The wreck lay between 44 and 52 meters deep on a steep, rocky slope riddled with sand pockets.

Half of the staff members who aided in the excavation lived in a camp built into the southeastern face of the promontory, which the ship most likely hit, while the other half lived aboard the Virazon, INA's research vessel at the time. The excavation site utilized an underwater telephone booth and air-lifts.
The mapping of the site was done by triangulation. Meter tapes and metal squares were used as an orientation aid for excavators.

Since the completion of the excavation in September 1994, all efforts have been concentrated on full-time conservation, study, and sampling for analysis in the conservation laboratory of the Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology in Turkey.

Eleven consecutive campaigns of three to four months' duration took place from 1984 to 1994 totaling 22,413 dives, revealing one of the most spectacular Late Bronze Age assemblages to have emerged from the Mediterranean Sea.

The Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology, housed within the Castle of St. Peter, displays artifacts recovered during excavations, along with a replica of the vessel, in its section dedicated to Late Bronze Age shipwrecks, which also includes items from the Cape Gelidonya shipwreck.
Historical background
Dating

Peter Kuniholm of Cornell University was assigned the task of dendrochronological dating in order to obtain a date for the ship. A branch loaded on the ship was determined to exhibit tree-rings as late as 1305 BC, but given that no bark has survived it is impossible to determine if it had further, younger rings.

It has been assumed that the ship sank not long after that date. Kuniholm later cautioned that the low quality of the sample does not allow an "especially strong" dating. After a radiocarbon calibration of the entire Anatolian dendrochronological sequence, Kuniholm suggested a new date, ca.

conducted radiocarbon dating tests on several samples of plant material from the site. A sample from the cedar keel of the ship was construed as providing a terminus post quem for the construction phase.

Other samples, including perishable items from short-lived species, like rope and dunnage, were construed to have come on board the ship in the phase of the last voyage. The two phases constrained each other, and Bayesian statistics was used to produce date ranges of varying probabilities.
The most likely date of the sinking of the ship was rounded up to 1320±15 years.

Based on ceramic evidence, it appears that the Uluburun sank toward the end of the Amarna period, but could not have sunk before the time of Nefertiti due to the unique gold scarab engraved with her name found aboard the ship.
For now, a conclusion that the ship sank at the end of the 14th century BC is accepted.
Late Bronze Age "globalization"
The Uluburun shipwreck is a major source of information on the long-distance and maritime circulation of goods in the Eastern Mediterranean during the Late Bronze Age (ca.

1600-1200 BC), as it relates to a context of development of long-distance maritime trade, also documented in the contemporary archives of Ugarit and the Amarna Letters, as well as archaeological discoveries made at various continental sites and some other shipwrecks.

The Uluburun documentation agrees with other testimonies from the period on the long-distance circulation of goods, which indicate that it was multi-directional, marked by reshipments of goods from transit points, and an evident diversity.

Thanks to the richness and diversity of its cargo, the Uluburun shipwreck remains to this day the most eloquent archaeological testimony to the development of maritime trade in the Eastern Mediterranean during the Late Bronze Age. It documents, more specifically, the relations between the Levant and the Aegean world.

Two other shipwrecks from the same period documenting long-distance trade have been excavated: the one off Cape Gelidonya (Turkey) and the one off Cape Iria (Greece, Argolis), both later (ca. late 13th-early 12th century BC).
However, they yielded more modest and far less diverse cargoes: copper ingots for the former and Cypriot ceramics for the latter.

From a geopolitical standpoint, this period is marked by the partitioning of the Near East and the eastern Mediterranean among a few major powers exercising their suzerainty over smaller kingdoms, "great kings" who maintained diplomatic relations as attested by the Amarna Letters.

Egypt during the New Kingdom (the final part of the 18th Dynasty) exerted its dominance over most of the Levant, particularly the south, the land of Canaan, divided into several small kingdoms whose tumultuous political life is also documented by the Amarna Letters.
Archaeology testifies to a certain dynamism in the coastal cities, well integrated into trade networks, but not all of these kingdoms were prosperous.

The other major power in the region was the Hittite kingdom, who, after a period of decline, rose again and took control of the northern part of Syria, previously dominated by the kingdom of Mitanni, and also brought Egyptian vassals such as Ugarit and Qadesh under their rule.
